en: His mount was Kertulpar,
Ebegey rode at his side,
And great Kögöy was his wise counselor,
His closest companion.
None remained to answer him defiantly,
And no force remained to overwhelm him.
Dear Kenen became khan,
And wherever he looked was at peace.
His honor was high and his wrath was mighty;
He split a black hair with perfect justice,
Never tearing apart or dividing
Kin from enemy unjustly.
He never favored the wicked;
He arose as a blessed lion,
Generous in nature and broad of heart,
With fortune perfectly fulfilled.
Splitting a black hair with perfect justice,
He arose as an impartial warrior-sultan.
The envious burned with resentment,
And his many watchful enemies,
Without even fighting, despaired of life.
His name became known throughout the world.
While gray-wolf Kenen reigned,
His chief wife Gulayym
Saw her affairs blossom like flowers,
And her fortune surged and overflowed.
She bore two sons, named Kulansaryk
And Alymsaryk.
When she had given birth to them,
She said, “I have borne two sons;
My wings now span a fathom, my tail fills an embrace,
And I have taken my place among the people.
My Alym and my Kulan,
My fine young sons whom I behold with joy,
Will remain behind me.”
She rushed about, placing her hopes in them,
And, gazing upon the children,
Prayed that they would be her legacy.
She had ninety animals slaughtered for their feast,
Had the babies lulled with cradle songs,
And gave them rhyming names.
Her prosperity surpassed all others;
The festive banners rose like misty mountains.
At the feast for those two,
The uproar split the sky.
At that very celebration,
Every soul whose ears could hear
And whose eyes could see gathered together.
The treasury doors were opened,
And abundant wealth was scattered
Among those who had none.
Playful young lads
Scrambled to seize the gold,
Then traded the riches they gained
For walnuts.
They overflowed with delight;
It was a splendid revel.
The ruler of Chin-Machin,
Descendant of Khan Aydung,
Chyngtengir, khan of Beijing,
Descendant of Khan Kongurbay,
Was a khan enthroned upon gold.
The countless people of the forty Chinese tribes
He held within his palm,
Never letting them slip from his grasp.
His dread was like a steel bullet;
Among all mortal sons ever born,
No such scourge as he had existed.
The wrathful hero Chyngtengir
Tempered his mind and pondered a plan.
Of his storehouse with forty doors,
He had one door opened,
And scattered provisions so vast
That eighty years could not exhaust them.
He requisitioned every riding beast,
And worked every mule until its back was raw.
Asking what had happened to the khan,
He burdened the people’s hearts
And gathered every last one of them.
The people murmured and the army gleamed,
And when they stood encircling him,
His vast strength became apparent.
He donned dark-blue iron armor,
Wrapped himself in a blue cloak,
And took up a blue-gray shield.
Such was the splendor of his appearance,
With jewel buttons large as fists.
Rousing himself like a blue lion,
Chyngtengir strode forth,
Roaring with menace,
And summoned the wise men
Of the teeming Chinese host:
—Among the vast Chinese nation of forty khans,
Does anyone have news?
With six swift horses
And a letter small as a palm,
I sent riders through swirling dust,
Dispatching them four times around
The four corners of the world.
I sent scouts among the nations
And gathered news from the peoples.
Old Jangju among the messengers—
No other man is like him—
Traveled alone and saw the lands,
Rode alone and saw the nations.
He says Akjoltoy and Seytek,
Who dwelt in Ala-Too, are dead;
They have died and seen
The true abode from which none return.
Seytek has left an heir,
And the treasuries overflow beyond counting.
Those wretched Kyrgyz people
Have returned to their old encampment.
They have made Ala-Too their homeland
And made Kenen their hero.
His forefather was hero Manas Khan,
His grandfather was Semetey,
And his own father was hero Seytek.
He is not a hair’s breadth
Inferior to any of them;
He has risen like a mighty plane-tree banner
And taken command of all the realm.
Everyone whose ears have heard
And whose eyes have seen him
Has claimed him as their inheritance and refuge;
Those worthless people
Have taken him as their protector.
They say that Kenen has arisen,
And that Kenen’s army stands ready;
His wisdom is great and his wrath is mighty,
And his cunning surpasses that of all men.
The two khans Ebegey and Kögöy
Have risen with spears in hand,
Becoming friends in the saddle;
They have begun to share together
The pleasures of this deceitful world until death,
To die when fate overtakes them,
And, digging a deep grave and stamping it firm,
For one to bury the other.
They have united and begun their revels,
And all the wealth they gathered
They have heaped together in one place.
They have made great Talas a fortress
And hero Kenen its lord.
If we do not go and crush
The crowns of those men,
If we do not drive out the ancient fury
Of Ebegey and Kögöy,
Of hero Akjoltoy and Kenen—
Those four guardians of the people—
If we do not strike first,
And find a way to settle the score,
If we do not block their traveled roads
And drive out every last one of their people,
Breaking their steadfast backs
And stilling their unruly hearts,
Driving spears into their farthest reaches,
Destroying all who resist,
And making their mighty men burn;
If we do not enslave that wretched nation
And divide them by measure of the lash—
The messenger has come saying Kenen is renowned,
Bringing word
That an enemy ready to fight you
Now stands prepared.
If we do not advance and block his road,
Scatter all he has acquired,
And overrun his settlements,
Then slaughter the thoroughbreds bred in Beijing—
This is the secret your lord now declares.
Braid the thoroughbreds’ manes.
If you take off your boots, stretch out your legs,
And lie at ease in careless peace,
Then within five or six years
The renowned gray wolf Kenen—
The infidel who devastated the people,
Whose wrathful power spells the end of the age—
Look upon him here in Beijing!
Will he remain without picking a quarrel,
Will he stop without trading insults?
If he rules the people and commands a nation,
Will he not seek revenge upon
The Chinese nation of forty khans
For his khan-father, blood-shedding Manas?!
The great lords of the Chinese realm,
Finding Chyngteñir’s judgment fitting,
The strong men clad in armor,
The heroes wearing mail,
The champions dressed in stone-hard armor,
The boundless men in quilted coats,
The warriors who know their own worth,
Despairing of their lives like flies,
The many seething dignitaries,
Saying that an edict had come from the khan,
Ran up and down,
Surged right and left in turmoil,
Young and old together—
All of Kakan and Beijing—
The whole people now heaved like a flood.
He made ready in wrath;
Chyngteñir was a mighty lord.
Taking the aspect of a blue-maned lion,
His voice thundered like the sky,
He loomed like a gray mountain range;
Any man who tried to judge him
Would lose the thread of his reason.
His fierce mustache appeared
Like the scree of Mount Kap;
His eyes were like blazing flame,
His jewel button was as large as a fist—
Such was his splendid appearance.
The countless Chinese facing him
Could not bear to look him in the face;
Whoever saw him despaired of life,
And knew him for a blue-maned lion.
Such was Chyngteñir, khan of the Chinese realm;
Such was the command he gave.
From before that formidable hero-lord
The envoys came forth,
The imposing appraisers:
Critics who could judge from afar,
Spies who ranged across foreign lands,
Men who worked through cunning,
Men who knew how to gauge a people,
Men who loaded merchandise on camels,
Who traded gold and silver,
Traveling as merchants,
Who among the Kyrgyz of Ala-Too
Drew out their hidden secrets,
Who kindled fire between peoples,
Who watched from outside to learn
The extent and strength of a nation.
The keenest judge among these observers,
The critic Zhelzhetpes, arrived.
He gauged the strength of the Kyrgyz
And observed their gathered people.
To the khan and lord Chyngteñir
He reported everything without omission:
“I observed Kenen carefully,
That lion and tiger of a warrior;
I studied the hero closely.
He is dark without and resolute within.
He will not fold his hands and submit,
Saying, ‘We are your slaves.’
He is no boy who will yield to fortune,
Nor some witless nobody.
They are not a people who will submit to being driven,
Like the Shibe and Torgout;
Nor are they a multitude like the Chinese.
The Kyrgyz nation is no grass to be mown.
Hero-lord, heed my words.
Let us send between us as envoy
An unerring, broad-jawed orator,
A man whose speech is sweet as sugar,
Whose skill surpasses the wisdom of an age.
Let us send an envoy between us,
